ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: In the image, 9 black dots can be seen, arranged into a square dot array of 3 rows and 3 columns. Each row and each column has 3 dots, and the two main diagonals also each have 3 dots. Reasoning: If only 2 dots are removed, then 7 dots remain. Distributing these 7 dots among the 3 rows in the figure, by the pigeonhole principle, at least one row will have 3 dots left; and the 3 dots in the same row are on one straight line, so removing 2 dots is not enough. Therefore at least 3 dots must be removed. Next, explain that 3 dots are enough: for example, remove the upper-left corner dot, the center dot, and the lower-right corner dot. In this way, among the remaining dots, each row, each column, and the two diagonals have at most only 2 dots left. For this 3x3 dot array, the straight lines that can contain 3 dots are exactly these rows, columns, and diagonals, so at this time there will not be 3 remaining dots collinear. Therefore, at minimum 3 dots need to be removed.

raw_record.question_text: The diagram on the right shows nine points in a square array. What is the smallest number of points that need to be removed in order that no three of the remaining points are in a straight line?

method.method_draft: Read the picture as a 3x3 square grid of 9 points. The text asks for the smallest number to remove so that no 3 remaining points are collinear. Use a row pigeonhole argument: if only 2 points are removed, 7 points remain, and 7 points spread across 3 rows force some row to still contain all 3 of its points. So 2 removals cannot work. Then show 3 do work by removing the top-left corner, the center, and the bottom-right corner; after that, every row, column, and diagonal has at most 2 remaining points, so there is no line with 3 points.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as a regular 3x3 grid. The key bridge is that the only 3-point lines in this array are the 3 rows, 3 columns, and 2 diagonals, for 8 total lines. Any valid deletion set must hit every one of those 8 lines. With only 2 deletions this is impossible: the best case is choosing the center plus a corner, which still hits only 6 distinct lines, so some row, column, or diagonal is left untouched and still contains 3 points. Three deletions are enough: remove the upper-left corner, the center, and the lower-right corner; that hits all rows, all columns, and both diagonals, leaving no 3 collinear points.
